knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 4.2.8
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly describes Pearson and deviance residuals and one diagnostic use?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Pearson scales by fitted variance; deviance residual comes from deviance contributions. LRT is a formal test, not the residual definition.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Pearson: standardised (y-μ̂)/sqrt(Var); deviance: signed deviance contribution.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Collapsing residuals into LRT or omitting variance scaling.

choices.label: Pearson residual uses observed minus fitted scaled by the variance structure: (y minus μ̂) over sqrt(Var̂(Y)). Deviance residual comes from the signed contribution of observation i to deviance. Both help check fit, outliers, and patterns.
Running a likelihood-ratio test finishes explaining Pearson and deviance residuals because LRT and residuals are the same diagnostic object.
Pearson and deviance residuals equal (y minus μ̂) with no variance scaling in GLMs.
Deviance residuals apply only to Normal GLMs; Poisson and binomial models use Pearson residuals exclusively by definition.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 4.2.8
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly states the idea of a Pearson residual and a deviance residual for a GLM observation?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Residuals standardise or decompose deviance at observation level. LRT compares models or assesses acceptability, a separate object.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Pearson standardised discrepancy; deviance signed contribution. LRT is different.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Accepting LRT as finishing residual explanation.

choices.label: Pearson residual: (y minus μ̂) over sqrt(Var̂(Y)), a standardised discrepancy. Deviance residual: the signed contribution of observation i to the deviance. Both help check fit, outliers, and patterns. An LRT is a formal acceptability or model-comparison test, different from defining and using residual diagnostics.
Running a likelihood-ratio test finishes explaining Pearson and deviance residuals.
Pearson residual equals y minus μ̂; deviance residual equals log(y/μ̂) with no further definition.
Both residuals are defined only after acceptability tests pass; before that, residuals are undefined.

worked_example.title: Pearson and deviance residuals for a Poisson count
worked_example.problem_statement: One commercial policy has observed claim count y = 3 and fitted Poisson mean μ̂ = 6. Compute the Pearson residual r_P = (y − μ̂) / √V(μ̂) with V(μ) = μ. Then compute the Poisson deviance contribution d = 2[y ln(y/μ̂) − (y − μ̂)] and the deviance residual r_D = sign(y − μ̂) √d.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form the Pearson residual first; then d and the signed square root.

steps.label: Pearson residual
steps.explanation: Pearson residuals standardise the raw residual by the model standard deviation.

steps.label: Deviance contribution
steps.attempt_cue: Substitute into the Poisson deviance formula.
steps.explanation: The deviance contribution is always non-negative; the residual takes the sign of y − μ̂.

steps.label: Deviance residual
steps.explanation: Because y < μ̂ the deviance residual is negative.

worked_example.final_answer: Pearson residual r_P ≈ −1.2247; deviance residual r_D ≈ −1.3569.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Dropping the sign when forming the deviance residual, or using √V(μ) = μ instead of √μ for Poisson.
